author: Steam Discovery Research
disclosure: Original editorial synthesis from cited public evidence, not a first-hand interview, proprietary sales database or claim that the publications endorse our conclusions. Historical source dates and the current observation date remain separate.

articles.title: There is demand for FPS survival. That does not make “FPS Zomboid” a gap.
articles.deck: Five Steam comparisons point to an occupied market. The useful opening is a testable player decision—not another camera angle.
articles.thesis: Build a reason to choose your survival experience before building a larger survival world.

evidenceCards.label: VEIN
evidenceCards.definition: Historical peak concurrent Steam players · 2 November 2025; checked 3 September 2026.

evidenceCards.label: Road to Vostok
evidenceCards.definition: Copies sold on Steam reported by its developer on 25 April 2026. Refund treatment unspecified.

evidenceCards.label: 2025 OWSC cohort
evidenceCards.definition: Qualifying 1,000-review games / tag-approximated releases in HTMAG’s January analysis. Not a startup probability.

sections.heading: Start with the competitor that already has your pitch
paragraphs: “Project Zomboid, but first person” is useful shorthand for an emotional reference. It is not a defensible market claim. VEIN already presents first-person zombie survival with scavenging, crafting and a home to fortify. Its Early Access page separates playable power and water systems from future NPC and settlement plans. The competitor is real; some of its future breadth is not yet shipped.

That changes the research question. We do not need to prove that somebody likes this combination. We need to discover why a player would leave a familiar game, try ours and return for another session. Perspective identifies the shelf. The recurring decision identifies the product.

sections.heading: Demand exists at several scales—but these are different clocks
paragraphs: The selected SteamDB observations below show substantial activity, including both older sandboxes and 2026 release milestones. They are not a league table of launch quality. Project Zomboid’s peak occurs in 2026 despite a 2013 Steam debut; HumanitZ’s 2026 full release follows Early Access from 2023. An all-time peak preserves whichever event was largest, not the current size of a reachable audience.

Road to Vostok supplies a different kind of evidence: its developer reported more than 250,000 Steam copies by 25 April 2026. It is a solo, non-zombie FPS survival comparison. That supports investigating a solo audience; it does not prove that removing multiplayer from any zombie game improves sales. Neither the post nor the charts isolate the incremental effect of a marketing channel.

sections.heading: A high historical ratio can hide an expensive admission ticket
paragraphs: HTMAG’s 2025 table lists 15 qualifying survival-crafting games against 72 approximated releases. The numerator is manually classified after filters; the denominator relies on tags. We calculate 15 ÷ 72 = 20.83%, but the calculation does not fix the mismatch in how the groups were assembled. It also does not price the years of engineering, content and support required to join that cohort.

Our inference is practical: low apparent supply may partly reflect production difficulty. Do not rank a three-week idea by the genre ratio alone. Compare how many meaningful decisions your team can demonstrate, what the audience will assume from the store tags, and which promised features you cannot currently support.

sections.heading: Find the job inside the genre
paragraphs: The same survival label contains several reasons to play: getting competent at dangerous procedures, protecting a familiar place, improving a shared base, or telling a story about an avoidable mistake. Those motives overlap, but their production costs do not. A server community, a vehicle sandbox and a single consequential expedition are different products.

For our prototype, the proposed job is to make the player feel responsible for the next threat to their home. A shortcut makes carrying supplies easier; it also becomes a route for infected. Noise, persistence and barriers are established ideas. Our hypothesis is about concentrating those ideas into one understandable return trip, not claiming to invent them.

sections.heading: Make the proposed opening falsifiable
paragraphs: Recruit people who play these comparables, then record what they actually prefer: solo tension, co-op activity, construction freedom or simulation detail. Show the real scope before asking whether they are interested. Otherwise a positive response may be interest in the larger game they imagined.

A promising result is not merely “looks cool.” It is a player understanding the route trade-off, identifying their own contribution to the outcome and voluntarily trying another plan. If they only ask for cars, guns or multiplayer, that is evidence about audience fit—not an automatic backlog. If they understand the choice and still do not want another run, more streets are unlikely to fix the central proposition.

comparison.title: Five selected comparables · observations checked 3 September 2026

cells: 7 Days to Die · First-person; solo and multiplayer
Road to Vostok · First-person, single-player, map-to-map travel rather than one asserted continuous world

comparison.caveat: Reviews are SteamDB aggregate observations, not Steam's English score counts or copies sold. Peak CCU is simultaneous activity, not reach. This deliberately selected group supplies no market-wide denominator.

takeaways: Demand evidence supports a test, not a sales forecast.
Choose one recurring decision that a small build can prove.
Use fresh target-player behaviour to decide whether a second street is worth building.
falsifiers: Players expect a broad sandbox and reject the disclosed small-session promise.
The shortcut has no meaningful benefit, or its consequence feels scripted and unfair.
Only co-op-first players respond, while the actual solo slice fails to attract repeat play.

articles.title: 200,000 wishlists is a timeline, not a tactic.
articles.deck: A campaign total hides the product, preparation and overlapping channels beneath it. Here is how to extract a usable playbook without inventing organic attribution.
articles.thesis: Copy the evidence-building sequence—not the winner’s headline number.

evidenceCards.label: DREADMOOR · May 2026
evidenceCards.definition: Publisher-reported wishlist stock; approximately 70K existed when the publisher joined. Not a three-week acquisition result.

evidenceCards.label: Design and Conjure
evidenceCards.definition: Agency-reported wishlist additions during a week combining sponsored creator work and Next Fest. Publication date and budget not supplied.

evidenceCards.label: Guildrun · July 2026
evidenceCards.definition: Developer-reported median demo playtime in its early demo cohort. A different product and time window from the other cases.

sections.heading: The visible spike is the last frame of a longer film
paragraphs: A large wishlist total is easy to remember and difficult to reproduce. DREADMOOR’s publisher account describes several milestones across months, not a single winning post. The source combines playtesting, showcases, creator coverage, social work and paid traffic. Unpaid individual posts are compatible with a campaign that also spent money elsewhere.

The history continued: its official 16 July announcement reported more than 350,000 wishlists and a planned 6 October demo. That is a later stock milestone, not evidence that one showcase generated the entire increase. The complete game story preserves both dates instead of silently replacing the May number.

The portable lesson is sequencing: make a product milestone worth showing, prepare the assets and access, select audiences that recognize the promise, then inspect the response. A five-person team can copy that discipline. It cannot responsibly copy a reported outcome into its forecast without the starting audience, development history, spend and attribution data.

sections.heading: Keep three ledgers instead of one persuasive funnel
paragraphs: The attention ledger contains platform impressions and views. The intent ledger contains store visits and wishlists. The product ledger contains demo starts, completion and repeat play. Each answers a different question. A creator can generate a memorable clip that fails to bring interested players, while a modest specialist video can attract people who stay.

Do not draw a conversion funnel using a video’s lifetime views, a festival week’s wishlist additions and a later demo’s unique players. The time windows and populations do not match. Put missing values on the page. A blank attribution field is more useful than a tidy but fictional ratio.

sections.heading: The small agency case is an operations lesson, not a cost benchmark
paragraphs: Design and Conjure is useful because the work is concrete: creator selection, briefs, rates, contracts, assets and a short access window. The agency reports four participating creators and five sponsored pieces, but the wishlist week also includes Steam Next Fest. Without the budget and counterfactual, neither cost per wishlist nor creator-only lift is available.

For our team, readiness is the experiment. Can a relevant creator understand the hook and play a stable short build with minimal back-and-forth? That is a process the marketer and PM can improve before large reach exists. It also protects the two developers from a last-minute stream of bespoke build requests.

sections.heading: Choose a format that can reveal the decision
paragraphs: Guildrun’s developer interview describes strong specialist long-form interest and says short-form was not a major driver. Iron Nest’s interview describes early traction from short clips, followed by other formats as playtests, the demo and launch approached. Neither case establishes a platform rule for all games.

Our survival clip should establish a complete thought: I opened this route; it helped me; the same opening now creates danger. A longer creator session can then reveal whether that thought remains interesting after the joke. These formats have different jobs. A clip tests legibility and curiosity; a real run tests the game’s ability to support a story.

sections.heading: Steam attribution is narrower than marketing causality
paragraphs: Steamworks separates total, trusted and tracked UTM visits, and uses a 72-hour window for attributed actions from tracked visits. Privacy thresholds and browser or device transitions can leave gaps. Even a correctly attributed wishlist is not the counterfactual claim that the action would never have happened without that link.

Use campaign names that identify the channel, creative and build. Never put personal data into UTM parameters. Keep paid, unpaid and unknown spending explicit. Measure the actual in-demo decision separately: UTM Analytics does not tell you whether someone understood the fence choice or chose to replay.

sections.heading: What a three-week team should aim to learn
paragraphs: Start with a few audience-matched placements and two truthful cuts of the same gameplay. Record who saw which version where, and do not pool platform view counts into unique reach. If a creator declines, distinguish lack of fit, lack of time and a build problem where they volunteer that information; silence is not a measured rejection of the genre.

The first decision is where to invest the next week: fix the promise, fix the build or expand a channel test. A 100K–200K headline is not an appropriate success gate for this first slice. The useful asset at day fifteen is a repeatable loop, a comprehensible pitch and a log that makes the next experiment less speculative.

comparison.title: Questions the case headlines cannot answer

cells: Large wishlist stock plus dated campaign beats
Total spend, isolated channel lift and paid sales
Sponsored pieces, combined views and a festival-week wishlist result
Budget, creator-only lift and exact campaign edition
Demo engagement and developer-described channel experience
The counterfactual result without any specific channel

comparison.caveat: These are different games, phases and denominators. No cross-case conversion rate is calculated.

takeaways: Record product milestones before you attribute campaign outcomes.
Separate attention, intent and play behaviour.
Use short footage to prove the hook and long sessions to test its depth.
Unknown spend is not organic reach; attributed traffic is not causal lift.
falsifiers: Viewers enjoy the clip but cannot describe the playable decision.
Relevant visitors try the demo but repeatedly stop before the consequence.
A channel's apparent improvement disappears when build, window and audience are held more consistent.

articles.title: The survival demo has to earn its second street.
articles.deck: A convincing small loop is more useful than an unfinished small version of a huge game. Turn the research into one consequential expedition—and a decision about what to build next.
articles.thesis: Protect the player’s causal story first. Expand the environment only when another run is wanted.

evidenceCards.label: Team capacity
evidenceCards.definition: Our planning arithmetic: 15 workdays × two developers and one artist. PM and marketing time is additional, not programming capacity.

evidenceCards.label: Inkbound
evidenceCards.definition: Developer-reported split of solo/co-op runs in its historical postmortem—not a split of unique players.

evidenceCards.label: Freerunners · 2024 demo
evidenceCards.definition: Self-reported median playtime for an 8–10-minute demo. Useful context, not a survival-demo target.

sections.heading: A small map does not automatically make a small project
paragraphs: First-person movement, interaction, animation, enemy navigation, crafting, saving and multiplayer all carry integration costs even when the map is tiny. A one-room or one-street pitch only reduces the work if its rules also reduce the system surface. Iron Nest is a useful warning: its concentrated setting still followed just over a year of development by two developers, according to their interview.

Our production choice is deliberately narrower. Use a familiar engine and reusable controller pipeline. Keep one enemy archetype and one route flag. Craft at fixed sockets. Persist the short session, not an off-screen simulation. There is no claim that this recreates a mature survival sandbox; it creates evidence about one player promise.

sections.heading: The central mechanic needs a before, an after and an alternative
paragraphs: The fence is not interesting because it opens. It is interesting because opening it solves an immediate carrying problem, persists, and later changes an enemy approach. A viable longer route gives the player an alternative. Warning cues make the risk fair. The same physical opening links the choice to the consequence.

If the night merely spawns more enemies whenever a hidden flag is true, the prototype has tested a scripted punishment. If the fence saves no meaningful effort, it has tested an obvious wrong answer. Both versions can be easy to implement and still miss the hypothesis. The prototype needs enough agency that a second plan could plausibly produce a different experience.

sections.heading: Explain the purpose before adding variety
paragraphs: The trailer consultations for Sheepherds and Dosa Divas are useful craft references: one makes a basic action readable before extra features; the other connects actions to the character’s objective. Those are communication judgments, not proof of sales uplift.

Apply the principle inside the demo. Start with a weak barricade and a clear reason to leave home. Let the player return with something that visibly changes safety. Only then introduce the second trip and the consequence of the shortcut. A catalogue of loot is not a substitute for a reason to care about bringing it back.

sections.heading: Solo is a scoped hypothesis, not a universal market truth
paragraphs: Inkbound’s postmortem describes competing solo and co-op design needs, alongside an approximately 60/40 split of runs. That does not tell us the preference distribution of survival players. It does show why supporting both modes is a design commitment rather than a menu checkbox.

For the first sprint, solo protects the route-choice test from networking and group coordination work. Road to Vostok demonstrates that solo FPS survival can find buyers, but its different fantasy and development history prevent a direct forecast. Recruit solo-first and co-op-first people separately; a mismatch is useful evidence, not permission to add networking on day eleven.

sections.heading: Treat the final week as a learning and reliability budget
paragraphs: The GDD allocates ten of thirty developer-days to integration, performance and fixes. This is our estimate, not a benchmark from successful games. Its purpose is to protect a complete playable handoff. The artist likewise needs time to make threats and interactions legible, not just to produce more props.

Freerunners’ historical demo postmortem is a reminder to inspect the experience and promotional files, not only the visit totals. A compressed clip can misrepresent movement; a short first session can indicate many different things. Our tests therefore separate comprehension, completion, technical failures and voluntary replay. No single median playtime can answer all four.

sections.heading: A day-fifteen build is not automatically a day-fifteen Steam launch
paragraphs: Steam’s demo workflow has its own review checklist and requires the base-game store page to be public. The demo’s own upcoming phase is optional, but new-partner eligibility still needs checking. Valve describes typical review timing and recommends at least seven business days of allowance; review is not guaranteed to finish on a chosen date.

Plan an eligible, near-final candidate around day eight if the public Steam demo is the target. Otherwise make the committed deliverable a stable, explicitly labeled prototype and genuine footage. Do not force a rough public release simply to claim the deadline was met, or describe a planned demo as already playable.

sections.heading: Let the next investment be a question, not an automatic map expansion
paragraphs: At the end, classify the result. If people cannot finish because of bugs, fix the test. If they understand the decision but do not want another run, revise the proposition. If they voluntarily replay and describe a different plan, recruit a fresh cohort and estimate the next slice before committing to an open world.

The proposed GDD uses small, explicit decision gates so the team knows what evidence to collect. They are not statistically powered demand measurements. Passing them earns another experiment—not a revenue forecast, a publisher promise or a list of ten more systems.

takeaways: Scope systems as aggressively as geography.
Show a fair choice whose physical consequence persists.
Budget reliability and recruitment as work, not leftovers.
Separate build completion, Steam eligibility and market validation.
falsifiers: Both routes produce the same meaningful outcome.
A fair, understood choice still fails to generate voluntary replay.
The cost of a reliable core loop consumes the sprint before outside testing can begin.
